claim: Science is facing a "replication crisis" in which many experimental findings cannot be replicated and are likely to be false.
source: Science is facing a "replication crisis" in which many experimental findings cannot be replicated and are likely to be false.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to replication studies throughout the introduction.

claim: Unless a sufficient fraction of negative results are published, false claims frequently can become canonized as fact.
source: We find that unless a sufficient fraction of negative results are published, false claims frequently can become canonized as fact.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mathematical model presented in the paper, supported by computational results shown in multiple figures.

claim: Data-dredging, p-hacking, and similar behaviors exacerbate the problem of false claims becoming canonized as fact.
source: Data-dredging, p-hacking, and similar behaviors exacerbate the problem.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model extensions showing inflated false positive rates, with results presented in Figure 8.

claim: If negative results become easier to publish as a claim approaches acceptance as a fact, true and false claims would be more readily distinguished.
source: Should negative results become easier to publish as a claim approaches acceptance as a fact, however, true and false claims would be more readily distinguished.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model analysis with dynamic publication rates, shown in Figure 9.

claim: Large scale analyses have revealed that many published papers in fields ranging from cancer biology to psychology to economics cannot be replicated in subsequent experiments.
source: Large scale analyses have revealed that many published papers in fields ranging from cancer biology to psychology to economics cannot be replicated in subsequent experiments (Begley and Ellis, 2012; Open Science Collaboration, 2015; Errington et al., 2014; Ebrahim et al., 2014; Chang and Li, 2015; Camerer et al., 2016; Baker, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to replication studies across different fields.

claim: A claim is a fact because it is accepted by the relevant community, not because it accurately reflects or represents underlying physical reality.
source: Note that we consider facts to be epistemological rather than ontological: a claim is a fact because it is accepted by the relevant community, not because it accurately reflects or represents underlying physical reality (Ravetz, 1971; Latour, 1987).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to philosophy of science literature.

claim: The RNAi pathway is initiated by the Dicer enzyme which slices double-stranded RNA into short fragments of 20–22 amino acids in length.
source: Based on work with Drosophila cell lines and embryo extracts, one group of researchers made the claim that the RNAi pathway is initiated by the Dicer enzyme which slices double-stranded RNA into short fragments of 20–22 amino acids in length (Bernstein et al., 2001).
evidence: This is presented as an example of a scientific claim, supported by citation to the original research.

claim: Publication bias arises when the probability that a scientific study is published is not independent of its results.
source: Publication bias arises when the probability that a scientific study is published is not independent of its results (Sterling, 1959).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to foundational work on publication bias.

claim: In 2007, more than 80% of papers reported positive findings, and this number exceeded 90% in disciplines such as psychology and ecology.
source: One extensive study found that in 2007, more than 80% of papers reported positive findings, and this number exceeded 90% in disciplines such as psychology and ecology (Fanelli, 2012).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited meta-analysis study.

claim: The fraction of publications reporting positive results has increased over the past few decades.
source: Moreover, the fraction of publications reporting positive results has increased over the past few decades.
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation, with implicit reference to the Fanelli (2012) citation in the preceding sentence.

claim: In a 2008 meta-analysis of 74 FDA-registered studies of antidepressants, 37 of 38 positive studies were published as positive results, but only 3 of 24 negative studies were published as negative results.
source: For example, a 2008 meta-analysis examined 74 FDA-registered studies of antidepressants (Turner et al., 2008). In that analysis, 37 of 38 positive studies were published as positive results, but only 3 of 24 negative studies were published as negative results.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited meta-analysis of clinical trials.

claim: In the antidepressant study meta-analysis, an additional 5 negative studies were re-framed as positive for the purposes of publication.
source: An additional 5 negative studies were re-framed as positive for the purposes of publication.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from the Turner et al. (2008) meta-analysis discussed in context.

claim: Negative studies were published at scarcely more than 10% the rate of positive studies in the antidepressant meta-analysis.
source: Thus, negative studies were published at scarcely more than 10% the rate of positive studies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data presented from Turner et al. (2008) in the preceding sentences.

claim: In the model, researchers sequentially test a single claim until the scientific community becomes sufficiently certain of its truth or falsehood that no further experimentation is needed.
source: We explore a simple model in which researchers sequentially test a single claim until the scientific community becomes sufficiently certain of its truth or falsehood that no further experimentation is needed.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure developed by the authors.

claim: If the claim under scrutiny is false, then investigators obtain false positives with probability α.
source: For mathematical simplicity, we assume all tests to have the same error rates, in the sense that if the claim under scrutiny is false, then investigators obtain false positives with probability α.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: When the claim is true, investigators obtain false negatives with probability β.
source: Conversely, when the claim is true, investigators obtain false negatives with probability β.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: A true claim is more likely to generate a positive result than a negative one: 1-β>α.
source: We assume that, as in any reasonable test, a true claim is more likely to generate a positive result than a negative one: 1-β>α.
evidence: This is a model assumption based on standard statistical testing principles.

claim: Readers are unlikely to perform sophisticated Bayesian updating and instead form subjective beliefs in an informal fashion based on a general assessment of accumulated results.
source: In practice, these values may not be as well standardized or widely reported as would be desirable. Moreover, readers are unlikely to be this sophisticated in drawing their inferences. Instead readers are likely to form subjective beliefs in an informal fashion based on a general assessment of the accumulated positive and negative results and the strength of each.
evidence: This is a statement about realistic reader behavior compared to the idealized model.

claim: Readers fail to correct for publication bias in drawing inferences from the published data.
source: We assume that readers are unaware of the degree of this bias, and that they fail to correct for publication bias in drawing inferences from the published data.
evidence: This is a model assumption stated explicitly.

claim: It is usually impossible for a researcher to accurately estimate the degree of publication bias in a given domain.
source: Moreover, it is usually impossible for a researcher to accurately estimate the degree of publication bias in a given domain.
evidence: This is stated as a practical limitation in scientific practice.

claim: In the model, true claims are almost always canonized as facts.
source: In our model, true claims are almost always canonized as facts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model, demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Even as the probability of publishing negative results approaches 1, the risk of rejecting a true claim is low when evidentiary standards are lax, and negligible when evidentiary standards are strict.
source: Even as the probability of publishing negative results approaches 1, the risk of rejecting a true claim is low when evidentiary standards are lax (Figure 3A), and negligible when evidentiary standards are strict (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The predominant risk associated with publication bias is the canonization of false claims.
source: Thus we see that the predominant risk associated with publication bias is the canonization of false claims.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results showing asymmetric risks for true vs. false claims.

claim: False claims are likely to be canonized below a threshold rate of negative publication, and unlikely to be canonized above this threshold.
source: False claims are likely to be canonized below a threshold rate of negative publication, and unlikely to be canonized above this threshold.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: When the false positive rate α is 0.05, the false negative rate β is 0.4, and the evidentiary requirements are strong, a false claim is likely to be canonized as fact unless negative results are at least 20% as likely as positive results to be published.
source: For example, when the false positive rate α is 0.05, the false negative rate β is 0.4, and the evidentiary requirements are strong (yellow points in Panel 4D), a false claim is likely to be canonized as fact unless negative results are at least 20% as likely as positive results to be published.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: The probability of canonizing false claims as facts depends strongly on both the false positive rate and the false negative rate of the experimental tests.
source: Figure 4 also reveals that the probability of canonizing false claims as facts depends strongly on both the false positive rate and the false negative rate of the experimental tests.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: As error rates increase, an increasingly large fraction of negative results must be published to preserve the ability to discriminate between true and false claims.
source: As these error rates increase, an increasingly large fraction of negative results must be published to preserve the ability to discriminate between true and false claims.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Under most circumstances, the probability of canonization is relatively insensitive to initial belief.
source: Under most circumstances, the probability of canonization is relatively insensitive to initial belief.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: False canonization rates depend strongly on initial belief only when evidentiary standards are weak and experiments are highly prone to error.
source: False canonization rates depend strongly on initial belief only when evidentiary standards are weak and experiments are highly prone to error (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: When evidentiary standards are weak and experiments are highly prone to error, belief is a random walk without a systematic tendency to increase or decrease with each published outcome.
source: In this case, belief is a random walk without a systematic tendency to increase or decrease with each published outcome, and thus the odds of canonization or rejection depend most strongly on the initial belief.
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior based on random walk theory.

claim: When the false positive rate α is relatively low, increasing the evidentiary requirements reduces the chance of canonizing a false claim for negative publication rates above 0.1 or so, but below this threshold there is no advantage to requiring stronger evidence.
source: When the false positive rate α is relatively low (Figure 6A), increasing the evidentiary requirements reduces the chance of canonizing a false claim for negative publication rates above 0.1 or so, but below this threshold there is no advantage to requiring stronger evidence.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: When the false positive rate is higher, for negative publication rates below 0.3 or so, increasing evidentiary requirements actually increases the chance of canonizing a false fact.
source: When the false positive rate is higher (Figure 6B), the situation is even worse: for negative publication rates below 0.3 or so, increasing evidentiary requirements actually increases the chance of canonizing a false fact.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: As the distance between the initial state and the boundaries increases, the probability of encountering one boundary before the other depends increasingly strongly on the average change in the log odds of belief at each step.
source: Basic results from the theory of random walks suggest that, as the distance between the initial state and the boundaries increases, the probability of encountering one boundary before the other depends increasingly strongly on the average change in the log odds of belief at each step (experiment), and less on the random fluctuations in belief that arise from the stochasticity of the walk.
evidence: This is a theoretical result from random walk theory applied to the model.

claim: For false claims, if too few negative outcomes are published, then on average each new publication will increase the belief that the claim is true.
source: Critically, for false claims, if too few negative outcomes are published, then on average each new publication will increase the belief that the claim is true, because there is a high probability this publication will report a positive result.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: For true claims, under most circumstances the expected change in the log odds of belief is positive.
source: First, for true claims, under most circumstances the expected change in the log odds of belief is positive (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, illustrated in Figure 7B.

claim: On average, scientific activity properly increases belief in true claims, and thus the risk of incorrectly rejecting a true claim is small under reasonable evidentiary standards.
source: That is, on average, scientific activity properly increases belief in true claims, and thus the risk of incorrectly rejecting a true claim is small (under reasonable evidentiary standards).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results on expected change in belief for true claims.

claim: Questionable research practices including p-hacking, outcome switching, unreported multiple comparisons, data dredging, HARKing, data-dependent analysis, and opportunistic stopping or continuation can result in higher-than-reported false positive rates.
source: Questionable research practices of all sorts can result in higher-than-reported false positive rates; these include p-hacking (Head et al., 2015), outcome switching (Le Noury et al., 2015), unreported multiple comparisons (Tannock, 1996), data dredging (Smith and Ebrahim, 2002), HARKing—hypothesizing after the results are known (Kerr, 1998), data-dependent analysis (Gelman and Loken, 2014), and opportunistic stopping or continuation (Pocock, 1987).
evidence: This is a statement about research practices supported by multiple citations.

claim: Insufficient validation of new technologies or software problems can drive realized error rates far above what is expected given stated levels of statistical confidence.
source: Insufficient validation of new technologies, or even software problems can also drive realized error rates far above what is expected given stated levels of statistical confidence (see e.g. ref. Eklund et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about sources of error supported by citation to a specific example.

claim: Industry-sponsored clinical trials often allow the sponsors some degree of control over whether results are published, resulting in an additional source of publication bias.
source: Finally, industry-sponsored clinical trials often allow the sponsors some degree of control over whether results are published (Kasenda et al., 2016), resulting in an additional source of publication bias separate from the journal acceptance process.
evidence: This is a statement about publication practices in industry-sponsored trials supported by citation.

claim: An inflated false positive rate makes it much more likely that false claims will be canonized as true facts.
source: An inflated false positive rate makes it much more likely that false claims will be canonized as true facts (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the model extension with inflated false positive rates, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: When the nominal false positive rate is αnom=0.05 but the actual false positive rate is αact=0.25, even eliminating publication bias against negative outcomes and using strong evidentiary standards does not eliminate the possibility that false claims will be canonized as facts.
source: For example, suppose the false negative rate is β=0.2 and the nominal false positive rate is αnom=0.05, but the actual false positive rate is αact=0.25. Even eliminating publication bias against negative outcomes (i.e., ρ0=1) and using strong evidentiary standards does not eliminate the possibility that false claims will be canonized as facts under these circumstances (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the model extension with inflated false positive rates, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Authors, reviewers, and editors are all drawn to unexpected results that challenge or modify prevalent views.
source: However, authors, reviewers, and editors are all drawn to unexpected results that challenge or modify prevalent views—and for a claim widely believed to be true, a negative result from a well-designed study is surprising.
evidence: This is a statement about publication practices in science based on general knowledge.

claim: The probability of publishing a negative result may be higher for claims that are already considered likely to be true.
source: As a consequence, the probability of publishing a negative result may be higher for claims that are already considered likely to be true (Silvertown and McConway, 1997; Ioannidis, 2005)
evidence: This is a hypothesis about publication dynamics supported by citations.

claim: When the fluctuating asymmetry hypothesis was proposed in evolutionary ecology, the initial publications exclusively reported strong associations between symmetry and attractiveness or mating success.
source: For example, when the fluctuating asymmetry hypothesis was proposed in evolutionary ecology, the initial publications exclusively reported strong associations between symmetry and attractiveness or mating success.
evidence: This is an empirical observation about a specific case in evolutionary ecology, with implicit reference to citations in the following sentences.

claim: As time passed after the fluctuating asymmetry hypothesis was proposed, an increasing fraction of the papers on this hypothesis reported negative findings with no association between symmetry and attractiveness or mating success.
source: As time passed, however, an increasing fraction of the papers on this hypothesis reported negative findings with no association between these variables (Simmons et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an empirical observation about publication patterns supported by citation.

claim: A likely interpretation of the fluctuating asymmetry publication pattern is that initially journals were reluctant to publish results inconsistent with the hypothesis, but as it became better established, negative results came to be viewed as interesting and worthy of publication.
source: A likely interpretation is that initially journals were reluctant to publish results inconsistent with the hypothesis, but as it became better established, negative results came to be viewed as interesting and worthy of publication (Simmons et al., 1999; Palmer, 2000; Jennions and Møller, 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of publication patterns supported by citations.

claim: Dynamic publication rates can markedly reduce (though not eliminate) the false canonization rate under many scenarios.
source: Figure 9 indicates that dynamic publication rates can markedly reduce (though not eliminate) the false canonization rate under many scenarios.
evidence: This is a finding from the model extension with dynamic publication rates, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Even if it is difficult to publish negative outcomes for claims already suspected to be false, we can still accurately sort true claims from false ones provided that negative outcomes are more readily published for claims nearing canonization.
source: In particular, Figure 9 suggests that even if it is difficult to publish negative outcomes for claims already suspected to be false, we can still accurately sort true claims from false ones provided that negative outcomes are more readily published for claims nearing canonization.
evidence: This is a finding from the model extension with dynamic publication rates, illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The dynamic publication mechanism may play an important role in preventing false results from becoming canonized more frequently in practice.
source: In practice, this mechanism may play an important role in preventing false results from becoming canonized more frequently.
evidence: This is a speculation about real-world scientific practice based on model results.

claim: Publication bias creates serious problems in scientific inquiry.
source: In the model of scientific inquiry that we have developed here, publication bias creates serious problems.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the model results.

claim: While true claims will seldom be rejected, publication bias has the potential to cause many false claims to be mistakenly canonized as facts.
source: While true claims will seldom be rejected, publication bias has the potential to cause many false claims to be mistakenly canonized as facts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the model results.

claim: False canonization can be avoided only if a substantial fraction of negative results are published.
source: This can be avoided only if a substantial fraction of negative results are published.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results.

claim: At present, publication bias appears to be strong, given that only a small fraction of the published scientific literature presents negative results.
source: But at present, publication bias appears to be strong, given that only a small fraction of the published scientific literature presents negative results.
evidence: This is an inference based on empirical observations of publication patterns cited earlier in the paper.

claim: Presumably many negative results are going unreported.
source: Presumably many negative results are going unreported.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that few negative results appear in the published literature.

claim: In the model, there is no advantage to selective publication; in all cases treated, false canonization decreases monotonically with increasing publication of negative results.
source: In our model, we observe no advantage to selective publication; in all cases treated we find that false canonization decreases monotonically with increasing publication of negative results.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis across all parameter combinations tested.

claim: Decision theory affirms that in the absence of information costs, withholding information cannot on average improve performance in a decision problem such as the classification task treated in this model.
source: Decision theory affirms that in the absence of information costs, withholding information cannot on average improve performance in a decision problem such as the classification task we treat here (Savage, 1954; Good, 1967; Ramsey, 1990).
evidence: This is a theoretical principle from decision theory supported by citations.

claim: A decision-maker should use all the evidence already available, provided that the cost of doing so is negligible.
source: As Good (1967) notes, a decision-maker "should use all the evidence already available, provided that the cost of doing so is negligible."
evidence: This is a principle from decision theory supported by citation.

claim: Much of the publication bias observed in science can be attributed to authors not writing up null results, rather than journals rejecting null results.
source: Several studies have indicated that much of the publication bias observed in science can be attributed to authors not writing up null results, rather than journals rejecting null results (Dickersin et al., 1992; Olson et al., 2002; Franco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from multiple cited studies.

claim: Authors may be responding to incentives that the journals have put in place when they choose not to write up null results.
source: This does not necessarily exonerate the journals; authors may be responding to incentives that the journals have put in place (Song et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation of author behavior supported by citation.

claim: Authors may be motivated by reputational factors when deciding whether to publish negative findings.
source: Authors may be motivated by other reputational factors as well.
evidence: This is a speculation about author motivations based on general knowledge of academic incentives.

claim: It would be a very unusual job talk, promotion seminar, or grant application that was based primarily upon negative findings.
source: It would be a very unusual job talk, promotion seminar, or grant application that was based primarily upon negative findings.
evidence: This is an observation about academic practices based on general knowledge.

claim: Strengthening evidentiary standards does not necessarily help avoid canonizing false claims in the presence of strong publication bias.
source: In this paper, we have shown that strengthening evidentiary standards does not necessarily help.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model results shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the presence of strong publication bias, false claims become canonized as fact not so much because of a few misleading chance results, but rather because on average, misleading results are more likely to be published than correct ones.
source: In the presence of strong publication bias, false claims become canonized as fact not so much because of a few misleading chance results, but rather because on average, misleading results are more likely to be published than correct ones.
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior based on the analysis of expected changes in belief.

claim: One advantage of framing experimental results as continuous-valued instead of binary is that there may be multiple opposing directions in which a result could be considered positive.
source: However, one advantage of framing experimental results as continuous-valued instead of binary is that there may be multiple opposing directions in which a result could be considered positive.
evidence: This is a speculation about how continuous outcomes might mitigate publication bias.

claim: If there is truly no effect and publication bias exists, we would expect to see false positives in both directions, and meta-analysis would readily pick up the lack of a consistent direction of the effect.
source: But suppose there is truly no effect: what does publication bias do in this case? We would expect to see false positives in both directions. Meta-analysis would readily pick up the lack of a consistent direction of the effect, and (if the authors avoid mistakenly inferring population heterogeneity) it is unlikely that correlations in either direction would be falsely canonized as fact.
evidence: This is a speculation about how bidirectional effects might prevent false canonization.

claim: False claims might generate more conflicting results, or take longer to reach one of the evidentiary thresholds, which could lead researchers to move on to other problems and leave the claim as unresolved.
source: In practice, researchers can and do lose interest in certain claims. False claims might generate more conflicting results, or take longer to reach one of the evidentiary thresholds; either mechanism could lead researchers to move on to other problems and leave the claim as unresolved.
evidence: This is a speculation about how real-world research dynamics might differ from the model.

claim: Many false claims might simply be abandoned instead of being rejected or canonized as fact.
source: If this is the case, we might expect that instead of being rejected or canonized as fact, many false claims might simply be abandoned.
evidence: This is a speculation about an alternative outcome for false claims not captured in the model.

claim: In practice, it may require less certainty to discard a claim as false than it requires to accept the same claim as fact.
source: Another possible difference between the model and the real world is that we model the evidentiary standards as symmetric, but in practice it may require less certainty to discard a claim as false than it requires to accept the same claim as fact.
evidence: This is a speculation about how real-world evidentiary standards might differ from the model assumption.

claim: If evidentiary standards are asymmetric, the probability of rejecting false claims would be higher than predicted in the model, possibly with only a very small increase in the probability of rejecting true claims.
source: In this case, the probability of rejecting false claims would be higher than predicted in our model—possibly with only a very small increase in the probability of rejecting true claims.
evidence: This is a speculation about the consequences of asymmetric evidentiary standards.

claim: A number of new journals or collections within journals have been established to specialize in publishing negative results.
source: A number of new journals or collections within journals have been established to specialize in publishing negative results. These include Elsevier's New Negatives in Plant Science, PLOS One's Positively Negative collection, Biomed Central's Journal of Negative Results in Biomedicine, and many others (Editors, 2016).
evidence: This is a factual statement about recent developments in scientific publishing supported by citation.

claim: Simply publishing negative results on preprint archives such as the arXiv, bioRxiv, and SocArXiv may make these results sufficiently visible.
source: Alternatively, peer reviewed publication may be unnecessary; simply publishing negative results on preprint archives such as the arXiv, bioRxiv, and SocArXiv may make these results sufficiently visible.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative publication mechanisms for negative results.

claim: If researchers accrue scant credit or reward for their negative findings, there is little reason for them to invest the substantial time needed in taking a negative result from a bench-top disappointment to a formal publication.
source: In either case, we face an incentive problem: if researchers accrue scant credit or reward for their negative findings, there is little reason for them to invest the substantial time needed in taking a negative result from a bench-top disappointment to a formal publication.
evidence: This is an inference about researcher incentives based on general knowledge of academic reward structures.

claim: Negative results or even corrections of blatant errors in previous publications rarely land in journals of equal prestige to those that published the original positive studies.
source: At present, however, our experience suggests that negative results or even corrections of blatant errors in previous publications rarely land in journals of equal prestige to those that published the original positive studies (Matosin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation about publication practices supported by citation and authors' experience.

claim: Even after false claims are established as facts, science can still self-correct through the accumulation of inconsistencies with other facts.
source: A final saving grace is that even after false claims are established as facts, science can still self-correct. In this paper, we have assumed for simplicity that claims are independent propositions, but in practice claims are entangled in a web of logical interrelations. When a false claim is canonized as fact, inconsistencies between it and other facts soon begin to accumulate until the field is forced to reevaluate the conflicting facts.
evidence: This is a speculation about self-correction mechanisms in science not captured in the model.

claim: Results that resolve conflicts by disproving accepted facts take on a special significance and suffer little of the stigma placed upon negative results.
source: Results that resolve these conflicts by disproving accepted facts then take on a special significance and suffer little of the stigma placed upon negative results.
evidence: This is an observation about how certain types of negative results are valued in science.

claim: The facts that science denialists target are almost always very different from the types of facts modeled in this paper.
source: The facts that science denialists target are almost always very different from the types of facts we are modeling.
evidence: This is a clarification about the scope and limitations of the model's applicability.

claim: The model addresses small-scale facts of modest import that would be established based on one or two dozen studies and then considered settled.
source: We are modeling small-scale facts of modest import, the kind that would be established based on one or two dozen studies and then considered settled.
evidence: This is a description of the scope of the model.

claim: The reality of anthropogenic climate change, the lack of connection between vaccination and autism, and the causative role of smoking in cancer are supported by massive volumes of research and have been established despite well-funded groups with powerful incentives to expose any evidence that might give cause for skepticism.
source: The reality of anthropogenic climate change, the lack of connection between vaccination and autism, or the causative role of smoking in cancer are very different. Facts of this sort have enormous practical importance; they are supported by massive volumes of research; and they have been established despite well-funded groups with powerful incentives to expose any evidence that might give cause for skepticism.
evidence: This is a statement about well-established scientific facts based on general knowledge.

claim: The process by which false claims can become canonized as fact in the model would not operate under circumstances where facts are supported by massive volumes of research and established despite well-funded opposition.
source: The process by which false claims can become canonized as fact in our model simply would not operate under these circumstances.
evidence: This is a clarification about the limitations of the model's applicability to major scientific facts.

claim: Science has proven unparalleled in its power to generate useful models of physical phenomena among all institutions and methods that humankind have developed to make sense of the universe.
source: Of all the institutions and methods that humankind have developed to make sense of our universe, science has proven unparalleled in its power to generate useful models of physical phenomena.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of science based on general knowledge and historical evidence.

claim: The point of asking questions such as those in the present paper is not to de-legitimize science, but rather to improve the accuracy and efficiency of scientific inquiry.
source: The point of asking questions such as those in the present paper is not to de-legitimize science, but rather to improve the accuracy and efficiency of scientific inquiry.
evidence: This is a statement of the authors' motivation and goals for the research.
